analysis.title: The Pulse of the Market: Midterm Musings
key_insights: RBC (Lori Calvasina) keeps its 12-month S&P 500 price target at 8,150, set in mid-September. Four of five models pointed to gains of 10-14%, but the target is pegged to the valuation/EPS model. The target implies a gain of slightly more than 6% from the 10/22/26 close.

RBC remains on guard for a tier 1 pullback of 5-10% in the S&P 500 in coming weeks or months, which would put the index at 7,000-7,400. The S&P 500 was down a little less than 2% from its all-time high at the 10/22/26 close. Tier 2 (14-20%) is not the base case, and it would likely need a recession scare, an interest rate shock, or negative EPS growth.

Midterm scenarios for US equities: a split Congress (Republican Senate / Democratic House) is neutral to modestly positive, a Democratic sweep is neutral to negative, and a Republican sweep is positive. This rests on the September analyst survey and the historical playbook. RBC makes no call on the outcome and does not include any post-election Iran re-escalation in these estimates.

Historical S&P 500 average annual return under a Republican president: 13% with united Republican control, 7% with split control, 5% with united Democratic control. When the S&P 500 is up in both 3Q and 4Q of a midterm year, the following year averages only 6.2% (3.5% median). If 3Q or 4Q is down, the following year averages 16.9% (18.4% median). 3Q26 was up and 4Q26 is still open.

Betting markets favor a Democratic sweep, but the trend has flattened. The Cook Political Report expects the House to flip and calls the Senate a toss-up. Since the Iran war began, Democratic-sweep odds have correlated positively with 10-year yields (+73%), diesel (+85%) and gas prices (+50%). Odds for a Republican Senate / Democratic House split have moved inversely to all three.

RBC reviewed toss-up Senate and House campaign videos from August to mid-October. Affordability and inflation dominated (groceries, housing, utilities, fuel). Health care, drug prices and insurance also drew heavy attention. Democrats stressed the Iran war and anti-big-business and anti-Big Tech rhetoric. Republicans stressed taxes and immigration. Data center and AI topics ranked higher in House races than in Senate races.

RBC flags a risk to the consensus view that AI regulation is limited. Governors are on the ballot in data-center-heavy states (Texas, Ohio), and anti-data-center sentiment is bipartisan. If that messaging drives battleground results, Congress could act more than investors assume. In that case RBC would add Tech to the sectors to worry about under a Democratic sweep.

Sector tilts from the September RBC analyst survey. Republican sweep: Utilities (+2.00), Energy (+1.00) and Financials (+0.78) are the most positive, Tech is +0.60, and Consumer Staples is negative (-1.00). Democratic sweep: Utilities (-2.00), Financials (-0.67) and Energy (-0.60) are the most negative, and Consumer Discretionary is positive (+0.43). Split Congress: Health Care is the standout (+0.71).

RBC lists four main tactical risks: the Iran war, downward cuts to bottom-up consensus EPS, the midterms, and higher rates with new Fed hikes. For the war, it worries that companies' hedges and inventory buffers are running out, and that consumer confidence has stopped recovering. It also notes reports of possible re-escalation after the midterms.

RBC's valuation/EPS model uses 2.75% CPI, three Fed hikes, 10-year yield at 5% and a 10% haircut to consensus EPS (about $344 for 2Q27 trailing-4Q EPS, 9% growth versus 21% consensus). That gives a fair value of 8,158, rounded to 8,150. The stress test with 3% CPI, four hikes and a 5.25% 10-year gives roughly 7,917. The model points to a meaningful down market if yields reach 5.5% with more hikes and stickier inflation.

The 10-year yield rose about 137 bps from late February to 5.3% on 10/5/26 and has since fallen below 5%. Real yields hit a new year-to-date high in October. Earlier yield-rise episodes with moves of 91 bps, 118 bps and 168 bps ended in either a 5-10% drop or the market powering through. The 2022 move of more than 300 bps coincided with a 25% decline.

A new Fed hiking cycle has just begun. Around the last six first-hike episodes, the S&P 500 typically saw a drawdown of 8.2% to 14.2% (median 9.6%, excluding 2022's -25.4%). Lows came 1-3.5 months after the first hike, and the market rose through the end of each cycle. RBC's rates strategists forecast two more hikes over 12 months.

The Growth/Value trade has been linked to the 10-year yield since late summer. Growth outperformed as yields rose, and Value has caught a bid as yields fell. RBC sees a new phase of Value leadership and is reluctant to fight it. Elevated Nasdaq futures positioning looks to be starting to unwind. The top-10 names' market cap share (42.1%) now matches their net income share (42.7%).

The US has lagged non-US developed markets since October 7. RBC says the US/non-US trade is vulnerable to reversal on valuations and flows. US P/E is slightly above its 5-year average relative to non-US. Flows to Western European funds have stalled, so the signal is mixed. Resolution of the Iran war could support non-US leadership.

RBC stays neutral on small caps versus large caps and pushes back on shorts. Positives: net futures shorts are the deepest since 2015-16 and 2022 and are narrowing, the Russell 2000 NTM P/E fell slightly below its Iran-war trough, and ISM manufacturing and GDP forecasts have improved. Negatives: rate-hike expectations, weak fund flows, and slightly wider high-yield spreads.

Sector calls: Health Care upgraded to overweight in mid-October, since it is a natural destination when reducing Tech. Tech cut to market weight, mainly on valuation, with softer flows and slowing upward revisions in semiconductors. Materials cut to market weight. Overweight Financials and Health Care. Underweight Utilities. Energy, Industrials, Staples, Discretionary, Comm Services and REITs are market weight.

3Q26 reporting season is lackluster so far. With 13% of S&P 500 results in, 85% beat on EPS and 63% on sales, versus 86% and 77% in 2Q26. Upward EPS revisions for the S&P 500 are 51.3%, close to turning negative, and the Russell 2000 is at 45.5%.

Bottom-up consensus S&P 500 EPS is $353 trailing four quarters for 4Q26, up from $313 at the start of the year. Consensus growth is 27% for 4Q26 and 21% for 4Q27. After the 2018 tariffs and the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war, it was the following year's consensus that took the damage (2019 and 2023). RBC worries earnings risk from the Middle East conflict sits more in 2027 than 2026.

In the post-COVID era, the S&P 500 forward P/E has tended to fall when the rate of upward EPS revisions turns negative. RBC therefore warns that downward revisions could further compress multiples. The relationship broke down in the post-GFC period and held loosely around the Tech bubble.

The S&P 500 NTM P/E is 24.0x, in the middle of its post-COVID range (the 26-28x area has been the ceiling and 20-21x the floor). The Nasdaq 100 NTM P/E is 26.9x, the top-10 names' NTM P/E is 24.9x, and the Russell 2000 NTM P/E is 15.8x. RBC says the top-10 cohort doesn't tolerate a break above 30x NTM P/E for long. The relative P/E of the top 10 is again slightly above their relative long-term EPS growth.

Semis FY2 P/E has moved back above its five-year average, and upward semis EPS revisions are decelerating. Software valuations got close to GFC lows, and software revisions are around 50%. Within Financials, RBC favors Banks, Insurance and Consumer Finance, while Capital Markets revisions are weakening (it is watching private credit).

Earnings yield gap models: the NTM version is -0.9% and implies a 14.9% historical 12-month return. The FY2 version is -0.55% and implies +13.4%. A 10-year yield above roughly 6.2% (NTM) or above 5.56% (FY2) would move the model into ranges historically tied to negative returns.

Sentiment: AAII net bulls were -8.90% for the week to 10/22 and -5.60% on the four-week average. The four-week average maps to a historical average 12-month S&P 500 gain of 11.1%. The weekly reading fell below -24% at one point recently.

Macro backdrop: consensus real GDP is in the low 2% range (RBC Economics 2.3% for 2Q27 and 3Q27). If GDP forecasts slipped to 1.1-2%, RBC's model signal would drop to 5.7%. The September jobs report was below expectations but, in RBC economists' view, still consistent with a healthy labor market, and rate-hike expectations for October and December eased. UMich sentiment ticked down from 48.1 to 48.0, and the May low is still intact. Fed Chair Warsh took over on 5/22/26.

EPFR flows: US equity flows are choppy and close to neutral, Western Europe is stalling, and Canada is a bright spot. Health Care fund flows are strong. Consumer funds had their largest weekly outflow since 2022. Materials, Utilities and REITs also saw large outflows. Financials had a very small inflow, Industrials are in outflow, and Value is slightly better than Growth.

market_movers.rationale: RBC upgraded the S&P 500 Health Care sector to overweight in mid-October. It cites positive EPS and sales revisions, attractive valuations and strong flows. It is a natural destination when dialing down Tech.
RBC cut the S&P 500 Technology sector to market weight in mid-October, mainly on valuation. Weaker developed-market Tech fund flows and slowing upward revisions in semiconductors also contributed.
RBC cut the S&P 500 Materials sector to market weight in mid-October. EPS revisions turned negative and the sector saw its largest weekly outflow since 2022.
RBC stays overweight the S&P 500 Financials sector on positive EPS and sales revisions and reasonable valuations. Banks, Insurance and Consumer Finance look most compelling.
RBC stays underweight the S&P 500 Utilities sector on expensive valuations, a record weekly outflow since 2022, and the most negative midterm sensitivity in a Democratic sweep.

sector_views.rationale: Upgraded in mid-October. Positive EPS and sales revisions, attractive valuations, positive flows, and a positive tilt in a split Congress.
Positive revisions and reasonable valuations. Most positive tilt in a Republican sweep and negative in a Democratic sweep. Sensitive to any downgrade to the economic growth outlook.
Downgraded to market weight in mid-October because of valuation, weaker flows and slowing semiconductor revisions. Software valuations remain attractive.
Downgraded to market weight in mid-October. EPS revisions turned negative and flows were weak despite attractive valuations.
Expensive valuations, largest weekly outflow since 2022, and the most negative outlook in a Democratic sweep (survey -2.00). The affordability debate and the link to the AI trade are headwinds.
Best relative performer since late July with improving revisions and valuations. Tempered by sensitivity to war headlines and limited visibility.
Strong upward revisions but among the most expensive sectors, with negative fund flows and recent underperformance.
Revisions are negative, valuations are expensive again, and global consumer fund flows had their largest weekly outflow since 2022.
Attractive valuations but negative sales and EPS revisions. RBC prefers Staples over Utilities among defensives and rates Health Care as the favorite defensive.
Attractive valuations but negative EPS revisions. Interactive Media and Media look attractive.
Attractive P/FFO valuations but the worst underperformer since late July, with outflows and rate sensitivity.

earnings_insights: 3Q26 reporting season (13% of S&P 500 results in as of 10/21/26): 85% beating on EPS and 63% beating on sales, versus 86% on EPS and 77% on sales in 2Q26.
Russell 2000 3Q26 (4% of results in as of 10/21/26): 67% beating on EPS and 57% on sales, versus 65% and 65% in 2Q26.

Bottom-up consensus S&P 500 EPS on a trailing-four-quarter basis is $353 for 4Q26 (consensus estimate, vs $313 at the start of 2026), with 27% y/y growth for 4Q26 and 21% for 4Q27. Consensus revenue growth for 2026 is 13%.

Consensus 3Q26 S&P 500 EPS growth is 24.6%, 2026 growth is 28.2% and 2027 growth is 20.9% (consensus estimates). Energy has the most improved 3Q26 and 2026 growth rates, and Tech, Mag 7 and Health Care are strongest for 2027.

S&P 500 net income is expected by consensus to peak in 2026. The AI basket and Mag 7 are expected to out-grow the rest of the index through 2028. Small caps are expected to out-grow the AI basket in 1Q27.

risk_factors: Further escalation or a longer Iran war: inflation, consumer weakness, and downward GDP and EPS revisions, with companies' hedges and inventories running out.
Downward adjustments to 2027 bottom-up consensus EPS, as seen in 2019 and 2023 after earlier shocks. Outright profit contraction is associated with drawdowns of more than 10%.
Midterm outcomes and AI or data-center regulation backlash, notably in battleground governor races in Texas and Ohio.
Higher yields and more Fed hikes: a 10-year yield at 5.5% with stickier inflation would point to a down market in RBC's model.
Capex cycle concerns, including peak capex growth and AI regulation.
Layoff announcements in Financials, and a possible downgrade to the US growth outlook, which could hit Financials.
Widening high-yield spreads would hurt small caps.
charts_described: Page 8 lays out the four tiers of fear: tier 1 is a 5-10% drawdown (7,037-7,428), tier 2 is 14-20% (6,255-6,724), tier 3 is a recession or major shock with a median drawdown of 27% (5,317-5,708), and tier 4 is about 50% or more (3,909).

Page 52 gives the S&P 500 2Q27 fair-value grid: 8,158 at the current model input (2.75% CPI, 4.50% fed funds, 5.00% 10-year, 23.72x P/E, 10% consensus haircut), 7,917 in stress test 1, and 7,402 in stress test 3.
Page 109 shows the 2018 and 2022 midterm-year pre-election drawdowns: Consumer Staples and Health Care outperformed, while Tech and Consumer Discretionary underperformed.
Page 116 shows betting markets favoring a Democratic sweep (Polymarket), with a Republican Senate / Democratic House split in second place and declining.
Page 117 shows the correlation between midterm betting odds and 10-year yields: +73% for a Democratic sweep and -60% for a Republican Senate / Democratic House split.
vol_and_positioning: Asset manager positioning in US equity futures has been elevated but not euphoric, and has slipped recently.
Asset manager positioning in Nasdaq 100 futures is a bit below its peak and does not look oversold. RBC sees early signs of it moving lower.
Russell 2000 futures net shorts are the deepest in recent decades other than 2015-2016 and 2022, and they are narrowing.
AAII net bulls were -8.90% for the week to 10/22 and -5.60% on the four-week average, versus -2.90% and -7.23% the prior week.
High yield spreads (Bloomberg US corporate HY average OAS) have widened slightly, which normally hurts small caps relative to large caps.
The gap in the share of upward EPS revisions between the top-10 names and the rest of the S&P 500 is 59%, down from 60%. The top-10 reading was about 90% recently.
geopolitical: The Iran war: US equities have priced in de-escalation since late March. Companies' hedges and inventories may soon run out, and news reports point to a risk of re-escalation after the midterms.
US midterm elections on 11/3/26: scenarios of Democratic sweep, Republican sweep, or a Republican Senate / Democratic House split, with possible AI and data-center regulation consequences.
Political conditions in France make catalysts for European equities hard to identify.
Gold and Trump's net approval rating have a -78% correlation, per RBC's commodity strategist Chris Louney's view that uncertainty drives gold.

tension_points.bull_case: A Republican sweep is positive for equities. Historically a united Republican Congress under a Republican president has averaged 13%, the analyst survey is positive, and the outcome is low in expectations. A split is neutral to modestly positive on removed uncertainty.
tension_points.bear_case: A Democratic sweep is neutral to negative. The survey tilt is modestly negative, historical returns average only 5%, and betting markets already favor it. If AI angst drives the result, Tech and AI regulation could be hit.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Exit polling or post-mortem analysis showing anti-AI or data-center sentiment drove battleground results would challenge the consensus view that AI regulation risk is limited.

tension_points.bull_case: RBC's price target of 8,150 implies a gain of slightly more than 6%. Models point to 10-15% gains, and the earnings yield gap and sentiment signals are positive.
tension_points.bear_case: A new Fed hiking cycle, stickier inflation and 10-year yields at 5.5% would turn RBC's model to a meaningful down market. Hiking cycle starts usually coincide with 10% pullbacks.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 10-year yield rising toward 5.5% with more hikes and stickier inflation, or consensus EPS cuts well beyond the 10% haircut RBC already assumes.

tension_points.bull_case: Small caps are cheap and underowned, with deep and narrowing futures shorts. The Russell 2000 NTM P/E is below its Iran-war trough, and consensus growth is stronger in 1H27.
tension_points.bear_case: Rate hikes and 10-year yields have driven underperformance since June 2026. Fund flows are weak, upward revisions are in negative territory, and high yield spreads are widening.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further high-yield spread widening or rising hike expectations would be a negative for small caps.
